Spring 1 founding year (11 Jan to 8 Feb 2027) includes the bridge weeks.

lessons.title: Bridge: Phase 5 alternatives ay, ou, ie, ea
lessons.bigQuestion: How do I choose between two spellings of one sound?
objectives: To read and spell words with ay, ou, ie, ea
successCriteria: All: say the sound for ay, ou, ie, ea
Most: read and spell words with the new sounds
Some: read a whole sentence with the new sounds and explain what it means
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: materials and mixtures (Will It Degrade?)

keywords.def: another way to write the same sound
two letters that make one sound
the letter or letters that write a sound

hook.text: rain and play both have the /ai/ sound. Why do you think one uses ai and one uses ay?
hook.a: ay usually comes at the end of a word; ai usually in the middle.

resources: Little Wandle Letters and Sounds Revised: Phase 5 review, grapheme cards (Year 2 bridge; school subscription)
Mini-whiteboard and pen
Reading book matched to the pupil's level (home reading)

teach.heading: Today's sounds
teach.note: Point to each grapheme: pupils say the sound, not the letter names, then read the words together, then faster. ay usually at the end of a word. ou as in cloud. ie as in pie. ea as in sea. Bridge week 2: Phase 5 alternative spellings.

teach.heading: Hinge: which one?
teach.note: Teams poll (or show the letter on a whiteboard on 3). Anyone who chose a wrong option gets a quick re-model before practice.

check.why: tie has ie. tray has ay; tea has ea.

teach.heading: Read the sentence
teach.note: Model with a finger under each word. Pupils echo-read, then read alone. Ask one question about the meaning.

model.problem: Stay out of the way while I pour the cream.
model.answer: Keep back while cream is poured.

teach.heading: Spell it
teach.note: I say, you say, you write. Pupils hold up their board after each word.

model.problem: Spell: cloud

practice.model: Teacher goes through it first: point under each sound, say it, blend it, then read or write the whole word. Answer: stay, shout, tried, dream

independent.q: Core: write a word for each: ay, ou, ie, ea
independent.a: For example: day, out, pie, sea
independent.model: Labelled model to go through first (Spell: cloud): Say it: cloud | Count: c-l-ou-d (4) | Which /ow/? ou here | Write and check | Result: cloud

independent.q: Extend: sort: tray, rain, play, paint (ay or ai)
independent.a: ay: tray, play; ai: rain, paint

independent.q: Stretch: write a sentence with spray and cream
independent.a: For example: Spray the cream on the cake.

lessons.homework: Read aloud to an adult for 20 minutes and practise this week's spellings: play, cloud, pie, cream.
lessons.send: SEND: grapheme mat and fewer words with more repetition. EAL: say each word in a spoken sentence first. Stretch: read: daydream, outside, cupcake.

lessons.title: The sounds ie and ea
objectives: Read and spell words with ie and ea
Know that ea can say /ee/ or /e/

keywords.def: a way to spell /igh/ in words like pie
two letters that can say /ee/ (eat) or /e/ (head)

starter: Read: day, play, out, house
Spell: stay
Which sound do ai and ay make?

teach.heading: ie says /igh/
teach.note: ie says /igh/ at the end of short words: pie, tie, lie. It also appears in tried, cried. Children read the words then spell them.

teach.heading: ea says /ee/
teach.note: ea says /ee/ in many words. Sound-talk: s-ea. Model reading with and without sound buttons. Link to meaning: ask ‘What do we eat for breakfast?’

teach.heading: ea says /e/
teach.note: ea can also say /e/ as in head. Teach children to try the sounds: /ee/ then /e/ and choose the one that makes a real word. Read: read (past tense) vs read (present).

teach.heading: Reading and writing
bullets: She tried to read the book.
teach.note: Read the sentences together. Ask children to circle the ie or ea words. Dictate one sentence for them to write and check.

practice: Read: pie, tie, eat, sea
Which two sounds can ea make?
Read: tried, cried, head, bread
Write: pie, sea, head
independent: Write three sentences using ie and ea words
Underline ea in two colours: /ee/ and /e/
lessons.homework: Practise reading and spelling pie, eat, head and ready.
lessons.send: SEND: sound button cards for ea. EAL: use picture clues. Stretch: write a sentence using both sounds of ea.

lessons.bigQuestion: Which spelling of a sound goes where in a word?
objectives: To read and spell words with oy, ir, ue, aw
successCriteria: All: say the sound for oy, ir, ue, aw
Most: read and spell words with the new sounds

keywords.def: another way to write the same sound
move a spoon round and round to mix
the letter or letters that write a sound

hook.text: Mixing words: which is the odd one out?
hook.a: turn: it has ur. The others have ir.

Mini-whiteboard and pen
Reading book matched to the pupil's level (home reading)

teach.heading: Today's sounds
teach.note: Point to each grapheme: pupils say the sound, not the letter names, then read the words together, then faster. oy at the end of a word; oi in the middle. ir as in stir: a mixing word! ue: try /oo/ then /yoo/. aw as in straw. Bridge week 2, day 2.

teach.heading: Hinge: which one?
teach.note: Teams poll (or show the letter on a whiteboard on 3). Anyone who chose a wrong option gets a quick re-model before practice.

check.why: stir has ir. turn has ur (same sound); star has ar.

teach.heading: Read the sentence
teach.note: Model with a finger under each word. Pupils echo-read, then read alone. Ask one question about the meaning.

model.problem: Stir the blue glue with a straw and enjoy the swirl.
steps: Spot: ir, ue, ue, aw, oy, ir
Ask: what do you stir with?

teach.heading: Spell it
teach.note: I say, you say, you write. Pupils hold up their board after each word.

model.problem: Spell: stir

practice.model: Teacher goes through it first: point under each sound, say it, blend it, then read or write the whole word. Answer: joy, third, clue, claw

independent.q: Core: write a word for each: oy, ir, ue, aw
independent.a: For example: toy, bird, blue, saw
independent.model: Labelled model to go through first (Spell: stir): Say it: stir | Count: s-t-ir (3) | Which /ur/? ir here | Write and check | Result: stir

independent.q: Extend: write stir, swirl, glue
independent.a: stir, swirl, glue

independent.q: Stretch: write two sentences about mixing slime
independent.a: For example: Stir the blue glue. Watch it swirl.

lessons.homework: Read aloud to an adult for 20 minutes and practise this week's spellings: toy, stir, glue, straw.
lessons.send: SEND: grapheme mat and fewer words with more repetition. EAL: say each word in a spoken sentence first. Stretch: read: birthday, enjoyment, statue.

lessons.title: The sounds ue and aw
objectives: Read and spell words with ue and aw
Read words with these sounds in sentences

keywords.def: a way to spell /oo/ as in blue
a way to spell /or/ as in saw

starter: Read: boy, toy, bird, girl
Spell: first
Which spelling is used at the end of a word: oi or oy?

teach.heading: ue says /oo/
teach.note: ue makes /oo/ (long oo) at the end of a word. Sound-talk: bl-ue. Children read the words then spell them.

teach.heading: aw says /or/
teach.note: aw makes /or/ and is used at the end or before n or l: lawn, crawl. Compare with or in fork. Read: draw, paw, claw.

teach.heading: Mixed practice
bullets: Which is ue? Which is aw?
teach.note: Children read pairs quickly. Say a word; they show ue or aw cards. Do 8-10 words quickly.

teach.heading: Reading and writing
bullets: I saw a blue paw print on the lawn.
teach.note: Read the sentences. Discuss meaning: ‘What did I see?’ Children write a sentence containing at least one ue and one aw word.

practice: Read: blue, glue, true, saw
Read: paw, draw, lawn
Choose ue or aw: bl__, dr__, tr__, p__
Write: blue, draw, glue
independent: Write 3 sentences containing ue and aw words
Draw a picture and write a caption using one of the words
lessons.homework: Look for ue or aw words in books and list three.
lessons.send: SEND: coloured cards. EAL: act out draw, saw. Stretch: write a story sentence using ue and aw.

lessons.title: Bridge: split digraphs a-e, e-e, i-e, o-e, u-e
lessons.bigQuestion: How does a split digraph change a word?
objectives: To read and spell words with a-e, e-e, i-e, o-e, u-e
successCriteria: All: say the sound for a-e, e-e, i-e, o-e, u-e
Most: read and spell words with the new sounds
Some: read a whole sentence with the new sounds and explain what it means
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: materials and mixtures (Will It Degrade?)

keywords.def: two letters that make one sound, with a consonant in between
a, e, i, o, u
a line under the word joining the two parts

hook.text: slim, slime. tub, tube. What does the e at the end do?
hook.a: It changes the vowel sound: short i to /igh/, short u to /yoo/.

resources: Little Wandle Letters and Sounds Revised: Phase 5 review, grapheme cards (Year 2 bridge; school subscription)
Mini-whiteboard and pen
Reading book matched to the pupil's level (home reading)

teach.heading: Today's sounds
teach.note: Point to each grapheme: pupils say the sound, not the letter names, then read the words together, then faster. Split digraph: link line from a to e. e-e is rare: these. i-e as in slime. o-e as in smoke. u-e as in tube. Bridge week 2, day 4.

teach.heading: Hinge: which one?
teach.note: Teams poll (or show the letter on a whiteboard on 3). Anyone who chose a wrong option gets a quick re-model before practice.

check.q: Which word has a split digraph?
check.why: slime: i-e split by m. slim has short i; sleep has ee.

teach.heading: Read the sentence
teach.note: Model with a finger under each word. Pupils echo-read, then read alone. Ask one question about the meaning.

model.problem: Make the white slime in a huge tube at home.
steps: Spot: a-e, i-e, i-e, u-e, u-e, o-e

teach.heading: Spell it
teach.note: I say, you say, you write. Pupils hold up their board after each word.

model.problem: Spell: shake
steps: The /ai/ is split: a, k, e

practice.q: Read: paste, these, rice, rope, cute
practice.model: Teacher goes through it first: point under each sound, say it, blend it, then read or write the whole word. Answer: paste, these, rice, rope, cute

independent.q: Core: write one word for each split digraph
independent.a: For example: cake, these, slime, stone, tube
independent.model: Labelled model to go through first (Spell: shake): Say it: shake | Count: sh-a-k (3 sounds) | The /ai/ is split: a, k, e | Write and check | Result: shake

independent.q: Extend: sort: shine, shin, cap, cape
independent.a: split digraph: shine, cape; short vowel: shin, cap

independent.q: Stretch: write a sentence with three split digraph words
independent.a: For example: I like to make huge cakes.

lessons.homework: Read aloud to an adult for 20 minutes and practise this week's spellings: shake, these, slime, smoke, tube.
lessons.send: SEND: grapheme mat and fewer words with more repetition. EAL: say each word in a spoken sentence first. Stretch: read: sunshine, cupcake, explode.

lessons.title: Split digraphs i-e and o-e
objectives: Read and spell words with i-e and o-e
Spot the e at the end that changes the vowel

keywords.def: split digraph that says /igh/ as in time
split digraph that says /oa/ as in home

starter: Read: cake, make, name, game
Spell: take
Add e: tap -> ?

teach.heading: i-e says /igh/
teach.note: Compare short i with long i by adding e. Read: kite, pine, time, like. Children say the word, then say the sound in the middle (/igh/).

teach.heading: o-e says /oa/
teach.note: Compare hop/hope, not/note. Read: home, bone, stone, rose. Link to meaning: ‘Home is where we say bismillah as we enter.’

teach.heading: Spelling the words
bullets: Write i, then m, then e
teach.note: Model segmenting: t-i-m-e has three sounds. Children spell time, like, home, note. Check final e.

teach.heading: Reading sentences
teach.note: Read the sentences and discuss. Children find i-e and o-e words. They write their own sentence with one of each.

practice: Read: kite, time, home, note
Add e: kit, hop, not
Read: like, mine, stone, rose
Spell: bike, hope, bone
independent: Write 3 sentences using i-e and o-e words
Sort words into two columns: i-e and o-e
lessons.homework: Write six i-e or o-e words and read them to a grown-up.
lessons.send: SEND: sort cards with pictures. EAL: group words by sound. Stretch: write a short description of your home using o-e and i-e words.

lessons.title: Split digraphs u-e and e-e, plus ew
objectives: Read and spell words with u-e and e-e
Read and spell words with ew

keywords.def: split digraph for /oo/ or /yoo/ as in cube and rule
a way to spell /oo/ as in new

starter: Read: kite, time, home, note
Add e: cub, tub
Spell: like

teach.heading: u-e words
teach.note: Compare cub/cube, tub/tube. In some words u-e says /yoo/ (cube, huge) and in others /oo/ (rule, June). Read and discuss. Avoid overload: read the sound by trying it.

teach.heading: e-e words
teach.note: e-e is the least common split digraph. Read: these, theme, complete. Many words with e-e are names or special words. Keep this short.

teach.heading: ew says /oo/
teach.note: ew makes /oo/ and is used at the end. Read: new, few, grew, flew. Compare with ue (blue). Put ‘blue, new, grew’ together as a set.

teach.heading: Reading and writing
teach.note: Read sentences with the class. Choose the words with u-e, e-e or ew. Children write a sentence with at least one of these.

practice: Read: cube, tube, rule, June
Read: new, few, grew, flew
Sort words by spelling: u-e, ew, ue (cube, new, blue, tube, flew, glue)
Write: rule, grew, these
independent: Write 3 sentences using words from today
Underline the spelling pattern
lessons.homework: Practise spelling cube, new, grew and rule.
lessons.send: SEND: use words with pictures. EAL: link to science (plant grew). Stretch: write a sentence with u-e, ew and ue.

lessons.bigQuestion: How many spellings do I know for one sound?
objectives: To read and spell words with wh, ph, ew, oe, au
successCriteria: All: say the sound for wh, ph, ew, oe, au

keywords.def: another way to write the same sound
a kitchen tool for beating and mixing quickly
the letter or letters that write a sound

hook.text: Kitchen puzzle: a tool for beating eggs starts with wh. A runny topping has au. What are they?
hook.a: whisk and sauce

pictures.find: tomato sauce in a bowl photograph

resources: Little Wandle Letters and Sounds Revised: Phase 5 review, grapheme cards (Year 2 bridge; school subscription)
Mini-whiteboard and pen
Reading book matched to the pupil's level (home reading)

teach.heading: Today's sounds
teach.note: Point to each grapheme: pupils say the sound, not the letter names, then read the words together, then faster. wh as in whisk. ph as in photo. ew: chew, new. oe as in toe. au as in sauce. Bridge week 2, day 3.

teach.heading: Hinge: which one?
teach.note: Teams poll (or show the letter on a whiteboard on 3). Anyone who chose a wrong option gets a quick re-model before practice.

check.why: sauce has au. saw has aw; sore has ore. Same sound, three spellings.

teach.heading: Read the sentence
teach.note: Model with a finger under each word. Pupils echo-read, then read alone. Ask one question about the meaning.

model.problem: Whisk the sauce, then stir the stew. What a photo!
steps: Spot: wh, au, ew, wh, ph
Read with expression: What a photo!
Ask: what do you do first?

teach.heading: Spell it
teach.note: I say, you say, you write. Pupils hold up their board after each word.

model.problem: Spell: whisk

practice.model: Teacher goes through it first: point under each sound, say it, blend it, then read or write the whole word. Answer: wheel, phonics, flew, goes

independent.q: Core: write whisk, sauce, stew
independent.a: whisk, sauce, stew
independent.model: Labelled model to go through first (Spell: whisk): Say it: whisk | Count: wh-i-s-k (4) | Which /w/? wh here | Write and check | Result: whisk

independent.q: Extend: write a word for each: wh, ph, ew, oe, au
independent.a: For example: when, phone, new, toe, sauce

independent.q: Stretch: write a question starting with what about a recipe
independent.a: For example: What is in the sauce?

lessons.homework: Read aloud to an adult for 20 minutes and practise this week's spellings: whisk, photo, chew, toe, sauce.

lessons.title: Four types of sentence
objectives: Recognise statements, questions, exclamations and commands
Write each type with the correct punctuation

keywords.def: a sentence that tells you something
a sentence that asks something and ends with a question mark
a sentence that shows strong feeling and ends with !
a sentence that tells someone to do something

starter: Say bismillah and spell: when, what
Which punctuation mark ends a sentence?
Add capital letters: the sun is hot

teach.heading: Statements
bullets: It ends with a full stop.
teach.note: Read examples. Ask for another. Each sentence starts with a capital letter and ends with a full stop. Practise writing two statements.

teach.heading: Questions
bullets: It ends with a question mark.
teach.note: Introduce question marks and question words: who, what, when, where, why, how. Model rising voice. Children write two questions about our class.

teach.heading: Exclamations and commands
teach.note: Exclamations begin with what or how and show strong feeling: ‘How kind you are!’ Commands tell people to do something (often start with a verb). Link to adab: polite commands with please.

teach.heading: Spot the type
teach.note: Read aloud. Children hold up cards S, Q, E, C. Discuss why. Common error: a question without a question mark; or ! used for everything.

practice: Add the correct punctuation: Where is my bag
Write one statement about your school
Sort 8 sentences into four types
Change a statement into a question: You are happy -> Are you happy?
independent: Write one sentence of each type about a trip to the zoo
Check punctuation with a partner
exit: What are the four types of sentence?
lessons.homework: Find one of each sentence type in a book and copy it.
lessons.send: SEND: sentence type cards with icons. EAL: practise reading with intonation. Stretch: write a short dialogue using all four types.

lessons.title: Nouns and expanded noun phrases
objectives: Identify nouns
Expand noun phrases with adjectives

keywords.def: a naming word for a person, place or thing
a describing word
a noun with words that describe it, like the tall green tree

starter: Name three things in the room
Add a capital letter and full stop: the dog barked
Which type of sentence is: Close the door?

teach.heading: Nouns
teach.note: Show a picture and ask children to name all the nouns they can see. Explain proper nouns start with a capital letter, names of people and places. Practise sorting: common vs proper.

teach.heading: Adjectives
teach.note: Show a plain picture of a bus. Add adjectives: big, red, noisy. Model asking: what colour? what size? what does it feel like?

teach.heading: Expanded noun phrase
teach.note: A noun phrase has a noun and describing words. Compare ‘a dog’ vs ‘a small, brown dog’. Children build their own phrases orally first, then in writing.

teach.heading: Use them in sentences
bullets: I saw a soft grey kitten.
teach.note: Children write sentences with expanded noun phrases. Check each phrase contains a noun and at least two adjectives. Celebrate precise vocabulary.

practice: Circle the nouns in: The girl has a red book.
Add two adjectives: a ___ ___ cat
Expand the noun phrase: a dog / the car / a house
Write three sentences using expanded noun phrases
independent: Describe the picture of a market with five expanded noun phrases
Underline the nouns
exit: Underline the noun in: a tiny green frog
Write a noun phrase about a bird
lessons.homework: Describe an object at home using two adjectives and a noun.
lessons.send: SEND: adjective word mat. EAL: pair adjectives with pictures. Stretch: build noun phrases with three adjectives and a comma.

lessons.title: Adjectives and describing sentences
objectives: Use adjectives to describe a person, place or thing
Write detailed descriptive sentences

keywords.def: a word that describes a noun
to say what something is like

starter: Write a noun phrase about a cat
What type of word is ‘happy’?
Say a noun that starts with sh

teach.heading: Describing with senses
teach.note: Model describing a mystery object using the five senses (use an object in a bag). Collect adjectives on the board. Encourage precise vocabulary.

teach.heading: Better adjectives
teach.note: Show how to improve weak adjectives. Children suggest alternatives. Use a word bank. Warn about overuse: one or two strong adjectives are better than five weak ones.

teach.heading: Write a description
bullets: The bird is small and bright blue.
teach.note: Model improving a sentence step by step. Children try with a picture. Link to appreciating Allah’s creation when describing nature.

teach.heading: Sentences with and
bullets: The sea is wide and blue.
teach.note: Teach joining adjectives with and. Show how it makes sentences richer. Children write two sentences using ‘and’ with adjectives.

practice: Give a better word for ‘nice’
Describe the object in the bag using one adjective
Rewrite with stronger adjectives: The big dog ran.
Write a description of a garden
independent: Write four sentences describing a place you like using adjectives
Circle the adjectives
exit: Underline the adjectives: The old, brown book was heavy.
lessons.homework: Describe your favourite fruit using three adjectives.
lessons.send: SEND: use picture cards and adjective banks. EAL: practise with real objects. Stretch: use similes: as bright as the sun.

lessons.title: Commas in a list
objectives: Know that commas separate items in a list
Write sentences with lists

keywords.def: a punctuation mark , used to separate items in a list
three or more items one after another

starter: Name the four types of sentence
Add the adjectives: a ___ ___ boy
Write a command

teach.heading: What is a list?
bullets: Use commas, and ‘and’ before the last
teach.note: Show a shopping list. Read it aloud with pauses. Explain commas show pauses between items. We use ‘and’ before the last item and no comma before it.

teach.heading: Writing a list sentence
bullets: I need a book, a pen and a ruler.
Do not put a comma before ‘and’
teach.note: Model writing the sentence. Common errors: using a comma at the end, or no commas. Practise orally first.

teach.heading: Spot the mistakes
bullets: I like red blue and green.
teach.note: Provide sentences without commas for children to correct. Discuss why the comma helps meaning.

teach.heading: Write your own
teach.note: Children write sentences about what is in their bag, what they saw at the market, or food on the table.

practice: Add commas: She had rice chicken and salad.
Write a list of three fruits
Rewrite with commas: We saw lions tigers and bears.
Write a sentence listing three things in your bag
independent: Write four sentences with lists of different items (food, clothes, animals, places)
Check commas with a partner
exit: Punctuate: I like dates figs and grapes.
Where do we not put a comma?
lessons.homework: Write a shopping list sentence about a picnic.
lessons.send: SEND: use list templates and picture cards. EAL: model with real objects. Stretch: use lists of adjectives in noun phrases.

lessons.title: Apostrophes for contractions
objectives: Understand that an apostrophe shows missing letters
Read and write contractions like can’t, don’t, I’m

keywords.def: a mark ’ that shows letters are missing or shows belonging
two words joined into one with letters missing

starter: Add commas: I packed a hat a coat and a scarf.
Write a sentence with a list
Read: when, what

teach.heading: What is a contraction?
teach.note: Show the full form and the short form. Point out where the apostrophe goes: in the place of the missing letter(s). Say them aloud, noting how we speak.

teach.heading: Common contractions
teach.note: Practise each. Note: it’s = it is (not belonging). Misconception: using its/it’s interchangeably. Spend time on this.

teach.heading: Make and spot
teach.note: Children practise matching long forms with short forms. Ask which letter is missing in each.

teach.heading: Use contractions
teach.note: Children write sentences using three contractions. Remind them that in careful writing, we still use full forms, but contractions are fine in speech and informal writing.

practice: What do two words become: do not?
Where does the apostrophe go in cant?
Match: can not / can’t, I am / I’m, is not / isn’t
Write the contraction for: she is, we are
independent: Write six sentences each using a contraction
Underline the apostrophes
exit: Write the contraction for: did not
Which letter does the apostrophe replace in I’m?
lessons.homework: Find three contractions in a book and write the long forms.
lessons.send: SEND: matching cards. EAL: model the spoken forms. Stretch: write a short dialogue with contractions.

lessons.title: Joining ideas with conjunctions
objectives: Use and, but, or, because, if and when to join ideas
Write compound and complex sentences

keywords.def: a word that joins words or ideas
a conjunction that gives a reason

starter: Which letters does the apostrophe replace in ‘isn’t’?
Add a conjunction: I like apples ___ pears.
Write a sentence with a list

teach.heading: And, but, or
bullets: I like tea but not milk.
teach.note: and adds, but shows a difference, or gives choice. Say sentences aloud; children identify the conjunction.

teach.heading: Because
bullets: I wore a coat because it was cold.
teach.note: Teach because by asking why questions. Children answer in full sentences: ‘I washed my hands because…’

teach.heading: If and when
bullets: If it rains, I take my umbrella.
When I get home, I pray.
teach.note: if shows a condition; when shows time. Children complete sentence starters. Link to practical life: ‘When I hear the adhan, I get ready to pray.’

teach.heading: Write your sentences
teach.note: Children complete the starters. Ask them to read back to check the sentence makes sense. Mark conjunctions.

practice: Join with and: I have a pen. I have a ruler.
Why? I took my coat because…
Join two sentences using because
Choose the conjunction: I like cake ___ I do not like jam. (but/because)
independent: Write five sentences using five different conjunctions
Underline the conjunctions

starter.q: Add commas: yoghurt honey oats and fruit

teach.heading: Features of a recipe
teach.note: Show a simple recipe card. Pupils name each part.

teach.heading: Model: Messy Fruit Pot
teach.note: Command verbs: Mix the oats.; Pour the yoghurt.; Sprinkle the fruit.; The verb comes first. Act each verb. Ask: who is the sentence talking to? (You, the cook.) Write live and make it on camera at the same time.

model.problem: How to make a messy fruit pot
steps: 4. Add the berries and stir gently.
Tip: Say bismillah before you eat it!
model.answer: Title, list, numbered steps with command verbs.

teach.heading: Hinge: which is a good step?
teach.note: Show me A, B or C.

check.q: Which step is written best for a recipe?
check.why: B starts with a command verb and tells the cook what to do. A is an opinion; C is a recount.

teach.heading: Your recipe
bullets: Check: does each step start with a verb?
teach.note: Pupils write their own recipe. This is the assessed piece: mark against the Year 2 writing checklist.

practice.q: Make it a command: You should stir it.
practice.model: Teacher works this one aloud: read the question, underline the key words, link it to today's rule, then give the answer in a full sentence: Stir it.

practice.q: Put in order: Eat it. Mix it. Pour it.
practice.a: 1. Pour it. 2. Mix it. 3. Eat it.

practice.q: Write a title for a recipe for a banana smoothie
practice.a: For example: How to Make a Banana Smoothie

independent.q: Core: write a title, an ingredients list and two steps
independent.a: For example: Fruit Pot. Ingredients: yoghurt, oats. 1. Spoon the yoghurt. 2. Add the oats.
independent.model: Labelled model to go through first (How to make a messy fruit pot): Ingredients: yoghurt, oats, honey, berries | 1. Spoon yoghurt into a cup. | 2. Sprinkle oats on top. | 3. Drizzle a little honey. | 4. Add the berries and stir gently. | Tip: Say bismillah before you eat it! | Result: Title, list, numbered steps with command verbs.

independent.q: Extend: write four numbered steps with command verbs
independent.a: For example: 1. Spoon... 2. Sprinkle... 3. Drizzle... 4. Stir...

independent.q: Stretch: add time words and a tip
independent.a: For example: Finally, stir gently. Tip: use ripe, juicy berries.

exit.q: Name two features of a recipe
exit.a: For example: ingredients list, numbered method

lessons.homework: Make your recipe at home with an adult, following your own steps. Did any step need changing?
lessons.send: SEND: recipe frame with picture prompts and a verb bank (mix, pour, add, stir). EAL: label the ingredients first. Stretch: add an adverb to two steps (stir gently, pour slowly).

check.why: animal ends in -al. Learn it as a word to remember.

teach.heading: Read the sentence
teach.note: Model with a finger under each word. Pupils echo-read, then read alone. Ask one question about the meaning.

model.problem: The metal pot fell off the pedal bin with a total crash.

teach.heading: Spell it
teach.note: I say, you say, you write. Pupils hold up their board after each word.

model.problem: Spell: metal

practice.model: Teacher goes through it first: point under each sound, say it, blend it, then read or write the whole word. Answer: capital, signal, sandal

independent.q: Core: write metal, pedal, animal
independent.a: metal, pedal, animal

independent.q: Extend: sort: total, bottle, tunnel, capital
independent.a: -al: total, capital; -le: bottle; -el: tunnel

independent.q: Stretch: write a sentence with metal and animal
independent.a: For example: The animal had a metal bowl.

exit.q: Name three ways to spell /l/ at the end of a word

keywords.def: the remains of a plant or animal from long ago, turned to rock
a child who learns at school
the letter or letters that write a sound

teach.heading: Hinge: which one?

model.problem: Spell: fossil

independent.q: Core: write pencil, fossil, pupil

keywords.def: letters added to the end of a word
the word we start with before adding a suffix
a word that describes a noun

hook.text: Mud, slime, crunch, stick. Turn each into a describing word for a messy mixture. What do you add?
hook.a: y: muddy, slimy, crunchy, sticky.

resources: Little Wandle Letters and Sounds Revised: Year 2 spelling materials, adding the suffix -y (school subscription)
Mini-whiteboard and pen
Reading book matched to the pupil's level (home reading)

teach.heading: Today's sounds
teach.note: Point to each grapheme: pupils say the sound, not the letter names. Read the words with sound buttons, then blend. Just add -y: stick + y = sticky. Short vowel and one consonant: double it (mud, muddy). Ends in e: drop the e (shine, shiny). Year 2 spelling: adding the suffix -y turns a noun into an adjective: stick, sticky.

teach.heading: Hinge: which one?
teach.note: Teams poll (or show the letter on a whiteboard on 3). Anyone who chose a wrong option gets a quick re-model before practice.

check.why: slimy: slime ends in e, so drop the e and add y.

teach.heading: Read the sentence
teach.note: Model with a finger under each word. Pupils echo-read, then read alone. Ask one question about the meaning.

model.problem: The muddy, lumpy mixture was sticky and slimy.
steps: Spot the -y adjectives: muddy, lumpy, sticky, slimy
Find the root words: mud, lump, stick, slime

teach.heading: Spell it
teach.note: I say, you say, you write. Pupils hold up their board after each word.

model.problem: Spell: muddy
steps: Short u, one consonant: double the d

practice.model: Teacher goes through it first: point under each sound, say it, blend it, then read or write the whole word. Answer: crunchy

independent.q: Core: add -y: stick, lump, rain
independent.a: sticky, lumpy, rainy
independent.model: Teacher does the first part aloud before pupils start, showing each step: sticky, lumpy, rainy

independent.q: Extend: add -y: mud, fun, slime
independent.a: muddy, funny, slimy

independent.q: Stretch: write a sentence describing a mixture with three -y adjectives
independent.a: For example: The gooey, lumpy, smelly mixture bubbled.

lessons.homework: Read aloud to an adult for 20 minutes and practise this week's spellings: sticky, lumpy, muddy, sunny, shiny, slimy.
lessons.send: SEND: grapheme mat and fewer words with more repetition. EAL: say each word in a spoken sentence first. Stretch: add -y to: grease, bone, frost, fuss.

lessons.title: Riddles and nonsense poems about food and materials (spoken)
lessons.bigQuestion: How can describing words make a riddle tricky but fair?
objectives: To write a riddle using adjectives and clues
successCriteria: All: write two clues for a riddle
Most: write a four-line riddle with adjectives and a question
Some: use rhyme or a -y adjective in a nonsense poem and perform it clearly
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: properties of food and materials

keywords.def: a puzzle poem that gives clues about something
words that end with the same sound, like jelly and belly
a silly poem with made-up or funny ideas
read aloud to an audience with expression

hook.text: I am cold and wobbly. I can be red or green. I shake when you poke me. What am I?
hook.a: jelly

pictures.alt: jelly, the answer to the riddle

resources: Tarbiyyah Primary English scheme of work, Muck, Mess & Mixtures (Friday writing): riddles and an acrostic poem about food and materials
Riddle frame: I am... I can... I feel... What am I?
A food item from the kitchen for clues (with an adult)
Mini-whiteboard and pen
Exercise book

teach.heading: Clue bank
teach.note: How a riddle works: Give clues, not the answer; Start easy or start hard?; End with: What am I?. Solve the hook riddle and talk about which clue gave it away. Pupils pick a food or material and collect clue words.

teach.heading: Model: a riddle
teach.note: Write live with pupils' help.

model.problem: Riddle about an apple
steps: I go crunch when you bite me.

teach.heading: Nonsense poem
bullets: Say it with rhythm, no tune
teach.note: Model a short spoken nonsense verse: A wobbly jelly in my belly, made my lunch box very smelly. Perform as spoken verse only.

teach.heading: Hinge: which clue is too easy?
teach.note: Show me A, B or C.

check.q: For a banana riddle, which clue gives the answer away?
check.why: B says the answer. A and C are fair clues.

practice.q: Write one clue for an egg
practice.a: For example: I have a hard shell.
practice.model: Teacher works this one aloud: read the question, underline the key words, link it to today's rule, then give the answer in a full sentence: For example: I have a hard shell.

practice.q: Turn into an adjective with -y: crunch, slime

independent.q: Core: write a riddle with two clues and What am I?
independent.a: For example: I am white and soft. I fizz in a bath. What am I? (soap foam)
independent.model: Labelled model to go through first (Riddle about an apple): I am round and shiny. | I am red or green. | I go crunch when you bite me. | What am I? | Result: An apple

independent.q: Extend: write a four-line riddle with adjectives
independent.a: For example: I am yellow and long...

independent.q: Stretch: write a two-line nonsense poem with a rhyme and perform it
independent.a: For example: A sticky bun stuck to the sun, which was not a lot of fun.

lessons.homework: Ask a family member your riddle. Could they guess it? Change one clue to make it fairer.
lessons.send: SEND: riddle frame with sentence starters and picture clues. EAL: choose a food from picture cards first. Stretch: write an acrostic for JELLY with a -y adjective on each line.
